rules: A case uses an entry only when its event type, firm type and size tier match the entry's scope. Matching is a lookup, not a judgement.
The case must carry a sourced direct cost when the entry has tiers, so the tier can be picked.
Ratios are shown per dimension with citation and scope. They are never added together or blended into one multiplier.
Market-value ratios (kind = market_value) are share-price losses at listed firms, not cash costs. Never add them to cost ratios.
If nothing matches, nothing is shown.

entries.measures: indirect cost / direct cost (workers' compensation) per injury
entries.scope: Construction injuries; OSHA calls them general estimates from limited research. Excludes fines, liability and goodwill.
entries.source: OSHA, $afety Pays Background (ratios from Business Roundtable, Improving Construction Safety Performance; Stanford study, year not stated on the page)
entries.tier_basis: direct cost of the injury, USD

entries.event: regulatory fine for misconduct harming customers or investors
entries.quote: reputational losses are nearly nine times the size of fines and are associated with misconduct harming customers or investors but not third parties
entries.scope: Listed firms; UK FSA and LSE enforcement. No reputational loss found where only third parties were harmed.

entries.measures: reputational loss / all legal and regulatory penalties
entries.quote: over 7.5 times the sum of all penalties imposed through the legal and regulatory system

entries.measures: equity value loss / estimated direct recall cost
entries.quote: The mean CER (-4, 5) is -6.13%, which is fully twelve times the mean relative direct cost of 0.53%
entries.scope: 32 drug and device recalls, listed firms, 1974-82. Drug recalls only, not autos. Jovanovic (2021) calibrates 6x as an average across later papers; that is his choice, not a published finding.
entries.source: Jarrell & Peltzman (1985), JPE 93(3): 512-536; quote from Stigler Center WP 033 (1984), p. 11

tiers.note: stated: total about twice direct above 200B

entries.scope: Modelled (adaptive regional input-output), Louisiana / Katrina. Regional economy, not a firm. No ratio is stated below 50B direct, so none is given there.
entries.tier_basis: direct losses of the disaster, USD

entries.measures: lost business (downtime, lost customers, reputation) as a share of total breach cost
entries.detail: 2025: lost business 1.38 of 4.44 USD M; detection and escalation 1.47; post-breach response 1.20; notification 0.39
entries.scope: 600 organisations, 17 industries, 16 countries, breaches Mar 2024-Feb 2025. Vendor-sponsored, consistent yearly method. 2026 average 4.99 USD M, no public category split.
entries.source: IBM / Ponemon, Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025, p. 13, Fig. 5

entries.range_note: 20% for jobs under $50k; up to 213% at the top of the range for very senior roles
entries.scope: 30 case studies from 11 papers, 1992-2007. Sizes one dimension; not a hidden/visible multiplier. Not for layoffs.
entries.source: Boushey & Glynn (2012), Center for American Progress, There Are Significant Business Costs to Replacing Employees

held_back.why: Primary text unreachable (withdrawn); secondary sources disagree on the denominator and trace it to four case studies.

excluded_folklore: Heinrich 4:1 indirect:direct accident cost (1931; no surviving data)
Bird iceberg $5-50 hidden per $1 (no traceable cost study)
SHRM 6-9 months of salary to replace (no primary study found)
Acquiring a customer costs 5-25x keeping one (no cited study; Reinartz & Kumar 2002 contradict)
1:10:100 / IBM Systems Sciences Institute 100x defect cost (course notes; Menzies et al. 2017 found no effect)
Gartner $5,600 per minute downtime (blog average, no method)
